subject: Social Science
chapter: History: Rise of Nationalism in Europe
text: Nationalism in Europe emerged in late 18th and early 19th centuries. French Revolution 1789 spread ideas of liberty, equality, fraternity. Napoleon spread Code Napoleon across Europe: standardised laws, abolished feudal privileges, equality before law. Congress of Vienna 1815 tried to restore conservative order under Metternich of Austria. Greek War of Independence 1821-1832: first successful nationalist movement; Greece became independent 1832 (Treaty of Constantinople). Romanticism promoted nationalist identity through vernacular languages, folklore, music. Germany: confederation of 39 states before 1871.

subject: Social Science
chapter: History: Rise of Nationalism in Europe
text: Unification of Germany: Otto von Bismarck used Realpolitik (blood and iron policy). Three wars: Denmark 1864, Austro-Prussian 1866, Franco-Prussian 1870-71. German Empire proclaimed at Versailles January 18 1871; Kaiser Wilhelm I became Emperor. Unification of Italy: Mazzini (ideology, Young Italy), Cavour (diplomacy, Prime Minister of Sardinia-Piedmont), Garibaldi (military, Expedition of the Thousand with Redshirts). Kingdom of Italy proclaimed 1861 under Victor Emmanuel II. Nationalism arose from: common language, history, culture, ethnicity; desire for self-governance.

subject: Social Science
text: France colonised Vietnam 1858; completed control 1884. French Indo-China included Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia. Economic exploitation: rice cultivation for export, rubber plantations, Vietnamese peasants became labourers. French schools taught French not Vietnamese. Phan Boi Chau: nationalist leader, founded Modernisation Society, led Dong Du (Go East) movement to Japan for education. Ho Chi Minh: founded Indochinese Communist Party 1930; organised resistance. Viet Minh: League for Vietnamese Independence founded 1941 by Ho Chi Minh. Dien Bien Phu battle 1954: decisive Vietnamese victory ending French colonialism. Geneva Accords 1954: Vietnam divided at 17th parallel.

subject: Social Science
text: Rowlatt Act 1919: detention without trial; caused nationwide protests. Jallianwala Bagh Massacre April 13 1919: General Dyer opened fire on peaceful crowd in Amritsar; hundreds killed; turned Indians against British. Non-Cooperation Movement 1920-22 (Gandhi): surrender titles, boycott civil services, courts, councils, foreign goods. Khilafat Movement: Muslims protested dismemberment of Ottoman Empire; Gandhi allied with Ali brothers for Hindu-Muslim unity. Chauri Chaura 1922: crowd burnt police station; Gandhi called off movement. Simon Commission 1928: all-white commission; boycotted with Simon Go Back protests; Lala Lajpat Rai lathi-charged and died.

subject: Social Science
text: Salt March / Dandi March 1930: Gandhi walked 240 miles from Ashram to Dandi to make salt; Civil Disobedience Movement began. People made salt, boycotted British goods; women participated extensively. Round Table Conferences 1930-32. Poona Pact 1932: reserved seats within joint electorate for depressed classes (Gandhi vs Ambedkar). Quit India Movement 1942: Do or Die; British arrested all leaders; most militant movement. Groups not joining Civil Disobedience: Dalits (some demanded separate electorate), some Muslims. Indian National Congress founded 1885. Early nationalists (Moderates): Gokhale, Naoroji. Extremists: Tilak, Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal (Lal-Bal-Pal).

subject: Social Science
text: Britain first to industrialise in 18th century. Proto-industrialisation: merchants put out work to rural households before factories. Key inventions: spinning jenny (Hargreaves), water frame (Arkwright), steam engine (James Watt 1781). Luddites: workers who smashed machines fearing unemployment. In India before British: thriving cotton textile industry (Dacca muslin, Calico from Calicut). British machine-made textiles ruined Indian artisans. First textile mill in Bombay 1854 (Cowasji Nanabhoy Davar). Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) at Jamshedpur 1911. During World War I Indian industries grew as British imports fell.

subject: Social Science
chapter: History: Print Culture and the Modern World
text: Johannes Gutenberg developed printing press with movable type around 1448 in Germany. First printed book was the Bible (Gutenberg Bible). Print revolution made books cheap and widely available. Protestant Reformation: Martin Luther 1517 used print to spread 95 Theses against Catholic Church. In India: printing press came with Portuguese missionaries in Goa 1556. James Augustus Hickey published first Indian newspaper Bengal Gazette 1780. Bal Gangadhar Tilak published Kesari (Marathi) spreading nationalist ideas. Vernacular Press Act 1878 tried to silence nationalist criticism. Print helped spread ideas about social reform, nationalism, and caste equality.

subject: Social Science
text: Resources: anything with utility and value that satisfies human needs. Classification by origin: Biotic (living: forests, fisheries) and Abiotic (non-living: rocks, metals, water). By exhaustibility: Renewable (solar, wind, water, forests) and Non-renewable (coal, petroleum, natural gas, minerals). By ownership: Individual, Community, National, International. Soil types: Alluvial (most fertile, northern plains, river deltas; khadar=new, bhangar=old), Black/Regur (Deccan plateau, ideal for cotton), Red and Yellow (peninsular plateau), Laterite (high rainfall areas, tea/coffee), Arid (sandy, Rajasthan), Forest soil (hilly areas).

subject: Social Science
text: Soil erosion and conservation: Sheet erosion (thin layer by water), Rill erosion (small channels), Gully erosion (deep channels, chambal ravines). Conservation: contour ploughing (along contours), terrace farming (hill slopes), strip cropping (alternating crops and grass), shelter belts (trees break wind). Resource planning in India: 3 stages: identification and inventory; evolving planning structure with technology; matching with national development plans. Sustainable development: meeting present needs without compromising future generations ability (Brundtland Commission definition).

subject: Social Science
text: India is mega-diverse: 8% of world biodiversity, 7% of world flora, 6.5% of world fauna. Forest types: Reserved forests (most protected), Protected forests, Unclassed forests. India forest cover about 22% of land (target 33%). Project Tiger 1973: launched to protect tigers; increased tiger population. Biosphere Reserves: Nilgiri, Sundarbans, Nanda Devi, Gulf of Mannar. Chipko Movement 1970s: villagers in Uttarakhand hugged trees to prevent logging. Sacred groves: traditional forest patches protected for religious reasons (Dev vans in HP, Orans in Rajasthan). JFM: Joint Forest Management between communities and Forest Department.

subject: Social Science
text: India has 4% of world freshwater. Multipurpose River Valley Projects: serve irrigation, hydro power, flood control, water supply, navigation. Bhakra-Nangal (Sutlej, Punjab/HP), Damodar Valley Corporation (Jharkhand/WB), Nagarjunasagar (AP), Sardar Sarovar (Narmada, Gujarat). Criticism of large dams: displace communities (especially tribals), submerge forests, interrupt ecosystems, silt accumulation. Narmada Bachao Andolan: Medha Patkar led protests against Sardar Sarovar Dam. Traditional water harvesting: Rajasthan khadins, tanks, baoris (stepwells); Bengal inundation channels; Tamil Nadu tank networks. Rooftop rainwater harvesting: mandatory in Tamil Nadu.

subject: Social Science
text: Types of farming: Subsistence (family labour, traditional methods, most output consumed); Commercial (HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation, machinery, for market); Plantation (single crop on large estate: tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane). Major crops: Rice (humid areas, eastern India); Wheat (cool moist winters, northwest plains Punjab/Haryana/UP); Cotton (black soil, Maharashtra/Gujarat); Jute (humid, West Bengal/Bihar, golden fibre); Sugarcane (UP largest producer); Tea (Assam largest, hilly slopes, well-drained); Coffee (Karnataka/Western Ghats). Green Revolution 1960s-70s: HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, irrigation; dramatically increased wheat and rice production; benefited mainly Punjab/Haryana/western UP.

subject: Social Science
text: Minerals: Metallic (ferrous: iron, manganese; non-ferrous: copper, bauxite, gold) and Non-metallic (limestone, mica, coal, petroleum). Iron ore types: Magnetite (highest iron ~72%), Haematite (most commercial ~60-70%). Coal: Gondwana formations in Jharkhand/Damodar valley, Odisha, Chhattisgarh. Types: Anthracite (best), Bituminous (most abundant), Lignite (lowest quality, Neyveli Tamil Nadu). Energy: Solar (India high insolation, Rajasthan/Gujarat best, National Solar Mission), Wind (Tamil Nadu coast/Muppandal, Rajasthan, Gujarat; India 4th largest wind power), Biogas (from cattle dung, agricultural waste, rural areas), Nuclear (Kudankulam, Narora, Kaiga, Tarapur use uranium/thorium).

subject: Social Science
text: Cotton textile: Mumbai is Cotton Polis (sea port, humid climate, capital, labour). Ahmedabad second largest. Iron and Steel: TISCO Jamshedpur (1907); SAIL plants: Bhilai (CG), Durgapur (WB), Rourkela (Odisha), Bokaro (Jharkhand). Cement: Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, AP major producers. IT industry: Bengaluru (Silicon Valley of India), Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai, Delhi, Mumbai. Industrial pollution: air (smoke/fumes), water (effluents in rivers), noise, thermal. Effluent treatment plants (ETPs) needed. Industrial location factors: raw material, labour, capital, market, transport, government policy, energy.

subject: Social Science
chapter: Geography: Lifelines of the National Economy
text: Roads: National Highways maintained by NHAI. Golden Quadrilateral: 6-lane superhighway connecting Delhi-Mumbai-Chennai-Kolkata (5846 km). Railways: 7335 stations, 67368 route km, one of world largest networks. Metro rail in major cities. Konkan Railway along west coast. National Waterways: NW1 Allahabad-Haldia on Ganga (1620 km), NW2 Sadiya-Dhubri on Brahmaputra (891 km). Major ports: Mumbai (largest, natural deep harbour), JNPT Navi Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata (riverine), Paradip, Vishakhapatnam, Kochi. Airways: Indira Gandhi International Airport Delhi, Chhatrapati Shivaji Mumbai. Communication: India second-largest telecom network; mobile subscribers exceed fixed lines; BharatNet expanding internet.

subject: Social Science
text: Power sharing is distribution of political power to prevent concentration. Belgium: Dutch-speaking Flemish 59%, French-speaking Walloons 40%, German-speaking minority. Solution: equal cabinet representation (4 Dutch + 4 French), community government for language groups. Avoided civil war. Sri Lanka: Sinhala 74% majority. Sinhala Only Act 1956 marginalised Tamils. Tamils demanded Tamil Eelam (separate state). Civil war for decades; ended 2009. Lesson: accommodating minorities prevents conflict. Forms of power sharing: Horizontal (legislature, executive, judiciary with checks and balances), Vertical/Federalism (central, state, local), Social groups (reservations), Political parties (multi-party competition, coalitions).

subject: Social Science
text: Federalism: power divided between central and constituent units (states). Features: two or more levels of government, each with own jurisdiction, constitutionally guaranteed, changes require both levels consent, courts interpret constitution, financial autonomy at each level. Types: Coming together (USA, Australia, Switzerland; independent states join voluntarily, stronger states) and Holding together (India, Belgium, Spain; large country divides power, weaker states). India: strong central government. Three lists: Union List (97 subjects including defence, foreign affairs, banking, currency), State List (66 subjects including police, agriculture, trade), Concurrent List (47 subjects including education, forests, marriage). 73rd and 74th Amendments 1992-93: constitutional status to Panchayati Raj and urban local bodies.

subject: Social Science
text: Social differences arise from birth (gender, race, caste, religion) or choices. Overlapping differences: when one social difference reinforces another (e.g., Black people in USA were also poor and less educated - more likely to cause conflict). Cross-cutting differences: social groups cut across each other (e.g., Catholics in USA are both rich and poor - less intense conflict). Civil Rights Movement USA 1960s: Martin Luther King Jr. led non-violent protests for African American equality. Mexico Olympics 1968: Tommie Smith and John Carlos gave black power salute. Suffragette movement: women fought for voting rights; 19th Amendment USA 1920 gave women voting rights. In India, women have formal equality but discrimination persists in practice.

subject: Social Science
text: Sex is biological; gender is socially constructed. Patriarchy: male-dominated society. Women in India: lower literacy, higher dropout rates, fewer in paid work, low political representation (about 15% in Parliament). 1/3 seats reserved for women in local bodies. Communalism: belief that own religion is superior; political mobilisation on religious lines; leads to riots and conflict. Secularism: equal treatment of all religions by state, no state religion. Caste system: hierarchical Hindu social division based on birth. Article 17 of Indian Constitution abolished untouchability. Reservations for SC/ST in education, jobs, Parliament. Mandal Commission recommended 27% reservation for OBCs in central government jobs.

subject: Social Science
text: Nepal democracy movement 2006: King Gyanendra dismissed parliament; seven political parties (SPA) allied with Maoists; mass protests; King conceded democracy; constituent assembly elections 2008. Bolivia water war 2000: government gave Cochabamba water supply to private multinational; prices tripled; protests led by FEDECOR; privatisation reversed. Both movements succeeded through popular mobilisation and alliances. Pressure groups: organisations influencing government without contesting elections. Sectional groups: FICCI (industrialists), INTUC (trade union), BKU (farmers), doctors and lawyers associations. Public interest groups: BAMCEF, Narmada Bachao Andolan, RTI movement. Pressure group methods: lobbying, petitions, strikes, hartals, media campaigns, PILs.

subject: Social Science
text: Development: improvement in living conditions and quality of life. Different people have different development goals: girl wants equal rights; farmer wants better prices; tribesperson wants forest access. Material goals: income, consumption. Non-material goals: freedom, security, respect, equality. Conflicting goals: dam benefits city people but displaces tribals. Per capita income: total national income divided by population; used to compare countries. World Bank classification by per capita income: Low income, Lower Middle income (India), Upper Middle income, High income. HDI (Human Development Index): measures life expectancy, education (mean and expected years of schooling), and GNI per capita. Kerala has higher HDI than Punjab despite lower per capita income due to better health and education.

subject: Social Science
chapter: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
text: Three sectors: Primary (agriculture, fishing, mining, forestry - uses natural resources), Secondary (manufacturing, construction - processes raw materials), Tertiary/Services (banking, transport, insurance, education, health). India GDP share changes: Primary fell from 50% in 1950 to 14% in 2012-13; Tertiary rose to 60%. But primary still employs 46% of workers. Disguised unemployment: more workers in agriculture than needed; their removal would not reduce output. Common in Indian agriculture and unorganised sector. Organised sector: registered with government, fixed hours, paid leave, provident fund, ESI. Unorganised sector: not regulated, irregular employment, low wages, no benefits (most Indian workers). MGNREGA 2005: guarantees 100 days paid work per year to rural households.

subject: Social Science
text: Barter system required double coincidence of wants. Money as medium of exchange eliminates this problem. Functions of money: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value, standard of deferred payment. Modern currency: fiat money issued by RBI in India; legal tender not backed by gold. Credit/loan: agreement to receive goods or money now and pay later. Collateral: asset pledged as security (land, house, gold). Formal credit: banks, cooperatives; lower interest rates, regulated by RBI. Informal credit: moneylenders, landlords, employers; higher rates (3-5% per month); no government supervision. About 50% of rural credit still from informal sources despite bank nationalisation. Self Help Groups (SHGs): 15-20 poor women; save together; give loans at low interest; SHG-bank linkage programme; promotes financial inclusion.

subject: Social Science
chapter: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
text: Globalisation: integration and interconnection of economies worldwide. MNCs set up production where labour and raw materials are cheap and markets are large. Trade barriers: tariffs (taxes on imports), quotas (limits on import quantity). Liberalisation: removal of trade barriers. WTO (World Trade Organisation): promotes free trade, reduces barriers between member countries. After India 1991 liberalisation: increased foreign investment, new IT/BPO jobs, increased exports. Disadvantages: hurt small manufacturers (local toys, batteries vs cheap Chinese goods), job losses in some sectors, inequality increased. IT sector benefited enormously: Infosys, TCS, Wipro, outsourcing from USA and Europe. SEZs: Special Economic Zones with tax benefits and relaxed labour laws for export-oriented industries.

subject: Social Science
text: Consumer: anyone who buys goods or services. Consumer exploitation: selling defective goods, overcharging, underweighting, adulteration. Consumer Protection Act 1986 (amended 2019): comprehensive law giving rights to consumers. Consumer rights: Right to safety, Right to be informed, Right to choose, Right to be heard, Right to seek redressal, Right to consumer education. Three-tier disputes system: District Commission (claims up to Rs 1 crore), State Commission (Rs 1-10 crore), National Commission (above Rs 10 crore). Quality marks: ISI (industrial goods: electrical appliances), AGMARK (agricultural products: spices, honey), Hallmark (gold jewellery purity, BIS certified), FSSAI (food products). Consumers must be aware, ask for receipts, and file complaints when exploited.
